title: Why everyone HATES Paul Carter (liftrunbang1)
summary: NH reviews coach Paul Carter's contrarian takes and agrees with most of them: deadlifts are poor back builders, deloads are unnecessary for bodybuilding, alcohol hurts gains, and chasing the pump is a myth. He adds his own pump-fatigue experiment. He rejects Carter's EMG-based claim that pullovers aren't a lat exercise, blaming bad form, and ends by telling viewers to take the good from contrarians and ignore the rest.
claims: The deadlift is a hip hinge that mainly grows the posterior chain (glutes, hamstrings, lower back); it is not a good overall back builder
Big traps on top deadlifters come from the sheer volume of heavy pulling; the deadlift is only a C-tier trap builder
Lats don't grow much from deadlifts just because they keep the bar close, any more than biceps grow from bench pressing
He once relied on deadlifts for his back; for lats do pull-ups and vertical pulls
The deadlift leaves the arms and small core details untouched, lacks an eccentric (a big part of each rep), and has a terrible stimulus-to-fatigue ratio

Anyone who has pushed the deadlift for 2+ years can't do it more than once, at best twice a week, which isn't enough frequency for a bodybuilder; deadlifting several times weekly just means you're still weak
The deadlift is the king of powerlifting lifts, not of bodybuilding lifts
He deadlifts only about once a month, purely to keep his Romanian deadlift progressing; the RDL is the better posterior-chain lift for bodybuilding
For a bigger back, do heavy vertical and horizontal pulls with a stretch and felt tension

The classic mesocycle (train far from failure, ramp volume until you can't recover, then deload and wait for supercompensation) is a poor way to build muscle, because growth stops once the stimulus is gone
Pre-deload blocks pile up low-intensity volume far from failure, then overshoot into junk volume your muscles can't recover from
Deload fatigue clears in about the first three days; the rest of the week nothing grows, and repeating this through the year wastes a lot of time
Saying you shrink during a deload is an exaggeration; muscle isn't lost that fast

Deloads appear nowhere in bronze, silver or golden era bodybuilding; the term spread about 20 years ago with the internet and the powerlifting boom, and it makes sense for strength athletes who peak, not bodybuilders
You can grow using deloads and some top naturals do, but they can't justify it; better fatigue and intensity management avoids needing them
Even an active deload, training far from failure, is wasted time for hypertrophy
People love deloads for the mental break and the PRs afterwards, but PRs after rest are expected; bodybuilding is about maintaining performance, not hitting PRs. If you like them, keep doing them
He can't stand fake-nice fitness influencers who play saints; Carter's bluntness is refreshing
Alcohol is the world's number one addiction, normalized so much that the non-drinker gets socially pressured and called weird
He is straight edge: no drugs and no alcohol
Even moderate alcohol (beer, wine, worse with liquor) impairs muscle building and gym performance; the effect is small but adds up
TRT youth clinics resemble 1970s American stress clinics that prescribed Quaaludes; he hopes they get cracked down on
Carter notes zero studies link the pump to muscle growth; the pump as a training goal is a myth
The pump is promoted mostly by enhanced lifters because anything works for them; bronze and silver era bodybuilders saw it only as a pleasant byproduct
Training for the pump means lighter weights and more reps: more metabolic stress and swelling but less mechanical tension, so you miss the long-term adaptation

Pump-fatigue experiment: find your 10RM curl (e.g. 130 lb), then do an empty bar (40 lb) for max reps; instead of the expected 50-70 reps you'll get about 30-40, because metabolic stress stops the muscle before real failure
If the pump dictates your whole training, you sabotage your gains
Beyond failure makes no sense: partials after full-ROM failure just move the failure standard; they have little benefit and can't be your main growth method
Contrary to Carter, the pullover is a lat exercise; Steve Reeves and many others built big lats with it
Carter cites EMG data showing pecs over twice as active as lats in the pullover, with lats at only about 8.4% even in the lowering phase
EMG is a poor predictor of growth: it shows more chest than lat activity on chin-ups and supinated pulldowns, and more ab activity on squats than on crunches or leg raises
The lats adduct and extend the arm, which is exactly the pullover motion, as in a pull-up
The pullover's active lat range is small (lats engage as arms go behind the head and peak at the stretch) but powerful enough to justify the lift

Most pullover critics do it wrong, lying flat with hips level with shoulders so there's no rib-cage or lat stretch; do it across the bench with hips dropped below it to open the thoracic spine and feel lats and serratus
Contrarians attack long-cherished ideas and dress the attack in jargon to look smart, e.g. Carter's sarcomerogenesis argument against lengthened partials
Many intermediates and advanced lifters report real gains from lengthened partials at almost no energy cost, so he encourages them even though he doesn't use them in his own method
He doesn't care what studies say about pullovers; his experience and that of his peers is what counts
Science-based lifting is disliked because it dismisses people's personal experience and instincts as worthless
With contrarian influencers, take what makes you doubt and grow, and ignore what only paralyzes or angers you
exercises: poor back/lat builder, bad stimulus-to-fatigue; use about once a month to drive RDL progress
better posterior-chain builder for bodybuilding than the deadlift
lie across the bench, drop hips below it, take arms deep behind the head into a rib-cage stretch
lat, serratus and rib cage builder; flat-on-bench version turns it into chest/triceps
bigger active lat range than the pullover
10RM, then empty bar for max reps
shows the pump limits performance before true failure
partial reps in the stretched position at the end of a set
reported gains at little energy cost
